pairs.rationale: The later love argument says that possessing all knowledge without love leaves its speaker nothing. That develops the knowledge/love contrast here; the food-idol setting and puffing-up/building-up images belong to chapter8 rather than the selected chapter13 verse.

Both qualify present knowledge. Here the self-confident knower has not known as he ought; chapter13 describes knowing in part and later knowing fully through mirror/childhood comparisons. They share the limitation theme without making every ignorant claim a prediction about the same future moment.

Both put being known by God alongside human knowing. Corinthians connects that recognition with loving God; Galatians corrects knowing-God language to being-known-by-God while warning about renewed enslavement to elements. The different conditions and warnings remain distinct.

The declaration that no God exists except one corresponds to Deuteronomy's none-beside-Him statement about the Lord. Deuteronomy speaks in the context of God's acts for Israel; Corinthians applies divine uniqueness to an idol-food discussion and separately calls an idol nothing.

The following yet-for-us statement supplies the explicit contrast to the concession about so-called gods and many lords: one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ. This is an internal contrast, not independent evidence that Paul endorses worship of rival deities.

Both attribute all things to divine origin and agency. Corinthians distinguishes one God the Father, from whom, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom; Romans uses the shorter from/through/to-Him doxology. Their actual named roles and formulas are retained rather than merged.

Both connect eating with the eater's religious understanding. Corinthians specifies prior attachment to an idol and a weak conscience being defiled; Romans says something is unclean to the person who reckons it unclean. The contexts and defiled/unclean descriptions are related rather than identical.

Food's inability to improve standing before God corresponds to Romans distinguishing God's kingdom from eating and drinking. Romans positively names righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit; Corinthians uses the no-better/no-worse comparison, not that full kingdom formula.

Both warn against making another believer stumble through one's conduct. Corinthians particularly names the knowledgeable person's authority and the weak; Romans commands against putting a stumbling block or snare before a brother. The authority/weakness wording is not added to Romans.

Corinthians describes a weak conscience being built up to eat idol-food through another person's temple example; Romans warns that a doubting eater is condemned because the eating is not from faith. These are distinct unsafe-eating scenarios, not a claim that Romans describes the same temple visit.

The weak brother for whom Christ died is being destroyed here; Romans commands not to destroy with food the one for whom Christ died. The shared food/brother/Christ-died warning is close, while statement and prohibition retain their different forms.

Sin against the brothers' weak conscience is called sin against Christ. Acts places Saul's threats against the Lord's disciples beside Jesus' why-are-you-persecuting-Me identification. The association with Christ corresponds, while conscience injury and violent persecution are different acts and occasions.

Both commend forgoing meat to avoid another brother's stumbling. Corinthians states Paul's conditional never-eat-meat resolve; Romans describes it as good not to eat meat, drink wine or do anything that makes a brother stumble. Wine and the broader list belong to Romans.

The later appearance account says Christ appeared also to the speaker and calls him an apostle whose labor depended on grace. It supplies internal testimony related to having seen Jesus and apostolic work, without repeating the freedom question or all the Corinthian-relationship claims here.

The Corinthians as the seal of Paul's apostleship correspond to his earlier claim to have become their father in Christ through the good news. Both appeal to the congregation's relation to his ministry, using different seal and father images rather than a literal biological or official seal claim.

The nearby questions about eating, accompanying wives and refraining from work provide concrete rights issues in this defense argument. This internal connection locates the defense within Paul's own reasoning; it does not supply a separate trial transcript or identify unnamed examiners.

The right to eat and drink has a practical counterpart in Jesus' instruction that workers remain in a house eating and drinking what is provided because the worker deserves pay. Luke gives mission-household instructions; Corinthians asks a question about apostolic rights.

Matthew's account of Peter's mother-in-law places Peter in a marital family relationship; John1:42 explicitly supplies the Cephas/Peter naming. This is a limited family correspondence: Matthew does not describe his wife's belief or traveling companionship, or establish the full right claimed for the other named groups.

Acts explicitly depicts Paul working at the same tentmaking trade as Aquila in Corinth. That is a concrete work example alongside Paul's question about the right to refrain from working; Barnabas is named only in Corinthians, and Acts does not independently describe Barnabas' arrangements.

Both use soldiers and agricultural workers as illustrations for ministry. Corinthians stresses ordinary entitlement to support or produce, including vineyard fruit and flock milk; Timothy stresses soldierly focus and says the laboring farmer shares first in the fruits. Their lists and particular lessons differ.

The next verse supplies the named law-of-Moses quotation after Paul's question whether the law also speaks. This is an explicit internal appeal-and-citation connection; the following ox question and human application are Paul's argument rather than extra words in the law itself.

The ox-not-muzzled rule directly corresponds to Deuteronomy's prohibition while the ox treads grain. Corinthians says while it threshes and follows with a question about God's concern; that interpretive question is not represented as another sentence of Deuteronomy25:4.

Both connect agricultural labor with a share in its yield. Corinthians names plowing and threshing in hope of sharing; Timothy says the laboring farmer must share first in the fruits. Timothy does not reproduce the ox quotation or Corinthians' for-our-sake interpretation.

Both connect receiving spiritual benefits with providing material support. Corinthians uses sowing/reaping in the relationship with its readers; Romans speaks of Gentile debt and service to the Jerusalem saints. The groups, direction of the particular collection and metaphors remain distinct.

The later letter describes preaching free of charge and not burdening the Corinthians, with support supplied from other Churches and Macedonia. That concretizes the unused-right policy here; bearing everything to avoid hindering the good news does not mean Paul never received outside support.

Deuteronomy assigns the Lord's offerings and specific sacrificial portions to the Levitical priests. This supplies concrete background for sacred ministers eating from the temple/altar, while the tribal inheritance rules and listed portions are not made a new identical regulation for every gospel worker.

Jesus' worker-worthy-of-pay instruction includes receiving household food and drink. It is a close teaching comparison for proclaimers living from the good news, while Luke's particular lodging directions and Corinthians' summary wording are preserved as different statements.

The later letter links not burdening the Corinthians with boasting that will not be silenced in Achaia. This corresponds to Paul's refusal to use the rights and lose his boast here; the interrupted better-to-die expression is not inserted into the later account.

Paul names necessity and woe if he does not proclaim. Jeremiah describes resolving not to speak the Lord's name, followed by unbearable fire-like burning in his bones. Both portray a burdensome speaking vocation, retaining different settings, imagery and messages rather than a shared physical experience.

The earlier passage calls the ministers stewards of God's mysteries who must be found faithful. That supplies a specific stewardship comparison for being entrusted here; the willing/unwilling and wages distinction belongs to this later argument, not the selected chapter4 sentences.

Both explicitly describe proclaiming the good news free of charge. Here that is Paul's stated wages and restraint in using his right; the later letter frames the same free proclamation as a rhetorical question about humbling himself and exalting his hearers.

Both put freedom beside voluntary slave-like service. Corinthians makes self-enslavement to all a way of winning more; Galatians commands service to one another through love and rejects freedom as a base for the flesh. Their recipients, motives and actual commands remain distinct.

Acts says Paul circumcised his companion because of local Jews who knew the companion's father was Greek. It offers a concrete accommodation toward a Jewish audience alongside the as-a-Jew policy; it does not quote that policy or call Paul under law, contrary to Corinthians' explicit qualification.

Both explicitly use law-of-Christ language. Corinthians qualifies accommodation to those without law with being within Christ's law; Galatians tells people to fulfill Christ's law by carrying one another's burdens. The missionary policy and burden-bearing instruction are related, not identical commands.

Becoming weak toward the weak corresponds to Romans' strong bearing the weaknesses of those without strength and seeking the neighbor's good. Corinthians gives winning/saving some as its aim; Romans emphasizes pleasing and building up the neighbor, without repeating every accommodation listed here.

The earlier refusal of support to avoid hindering Christ's good news provides a concrete example of doing things for that good news. This is an internal motive connection; sharing in it with others is the additional aim stated here, not an extra phrase in9:12.

Both exhort their readers to run a figurative race purposefully. Corinthians uses a stadium's one prize to urge obtaining it; Hebrews urges endurance with eyes on Jesus. The one-winner illustration is not imported as a claim that only one of Hebrews' hearers can be saved.

The imperishable wreath sought by the competitors is comparable to Timothy's promised crown of righteousness after the fight/course. Corinthians contrasts perishable and imperishable awards; Timothy names the righteous Judge and all who loved His appearing, rather than using the same self-control formulation.

Running and boxing with direction correspond to Timothy's fought-the-good-fight and finished-the-course images. Corinthians describes present purposeful effort; Timothy's speaker looks back on completion. The shared athletic language does not identify one literal race or boxing event.

Paul's concern that he might become disqualified after proclaiming to others corresponds to the later call for self-examination lest the readers fail the test. Corinthians' bodily-discipline image and the later faith/Christ-in-you test retain their different terms and addressed persons.

Exodus places the pillar of cloud between the camps and narrates Israel passing through the divided sea on dry ground. Those are the concrete narrative events recalled here; the all-our-fathers summary is Paul's wording rather than an added sentence of Exodus.

Exodus narrates Moses stretching his hand over the sea and Israel entering its dry midst. Corinthians interprets the cloud/sea experience as baptism into Moses; Exodus itself does not name this action baptism or describe the Israelites as immersed in the surrounding water.

Exodus identifies the unfamiliar wilderness substance as bread the Lord gave the people to eat. It supplies the food narrative behind Paul's spiritual-food description; the word spiritual and the shared-all emphasis are Corinthians' characterization rather than the selected Exodus wording.

Exodus depicts water coming from the Horeb rock for the people to drink. Corinthians calls the drink and rock spiritual, describes the rock as following and identifies it as Christ. Those additional identifications are Paul's typological reading, not explicit sentences about Christ or a moving rock in Exodus.

Numbers announces that the registered grumblers' bodies will fall in the wilderness, with Caleb and Joshua excepted from exclusion. That supplies concrete background for most being strewn over the wilderness; Corinthians summarizes God's displeasure rather than reproducing the registration and land-entry details.

Numbers describes intense craving, requests for meat and longing for Egyptian foods instead of manna. Corinthians treats the earlier desires as a warning against desiring evil things; that moral application is Paul's, not a claim that Numbers uses the identical general phrase or condemns every instance of hunger.

The eating, drinking and rising-to-play clause closely corresponds to Exodus32:6 after its sacrificial actions. Corinthians explicitly introduces it as written and uses it in an idolatry warning; the preceding offering details remain in Exodus rather than being added to the shorter citation.

Numbers links sexual immorality with Moabite women, idol-sacrificial meals and a deadly plague. The counts differ: Corinthians says twenty-three thousand in one day, while Numbers gives twenty-four thousand plague deaths. The link preserves both accounts without inventing a numerical reconciliation or importing every narrated action as a command to readers.

Numbers narrates speech against God and Moses followed by the Lord sending deadly serpents and many deaths. Corinthians names testing Christ and destruction by serpents. The serpent-judgment background is specific, while Christ is not silently substituted for an explicit personal name in the Numbers wording.

In the actual Greek-based Numbers17:6–14 division, grumbling against Moses and Aaron is followed by an outbreak and Aaron's intercession. This supplies grumbling/judgment background. Corinthians says destroyer; Numbers speaks of the Lord's wrath and the outbreak and does not name that agent with the same noun.

Both explain earlier Scripture as instruction for later readers. Corinthians stresses examples, admonition and the arrival of the ages' ends; Romans emphasizes perseverance, encouragement and hope. The purposes correspond without treating the added time statement and the hope explanation as identical clauses.

Romans tells the one standing by faith not to be haughty but to fear, warning that natural branches were not spared. That corresponds to the stand/fall self-warning here, with different olive imagery and an explicitly faith/unbelief comparison rather than the same historical illustration.

Both locate help within testing: Corinthians names faithful God providing a way out so the tempted can endure; Hebrews says the One who suffered when tested can help those being tested. The agency, temptation/test wording and particular promises remain distinct rather than one verbatim guarantee about every kind of affliction.

The command to flee idolatry corresponds directly to the instruction to guard oneself from idols. Corinthians addresses the beloved and develops sacrificial participation; John addresses little children. Their concise prohibitions are close while the surrounding explanations differ.

Both ask the readers to judge for themselves. Here they are addressed as wise before the cup/meal reasoning; chapter11 asks whether an uncovered woman praying is fitting. This is an internal instructional-form comparison, preserving the different subjects rather than making the judgments interchangeable.

The later meal tradition identifies the bread with Jesus' body and the cup with the new covenant in His blood, followed by eating/drinking as proclamation. That is specific internal context for participation in Christ's body and blood here; no unprinted explanation of the physical mechanism is supplied.

Both connect many people with one body. Here shared participation in one bread supplies the explanation; chapter12 develops the body's many members in relation to Christ. The bread image and the member image remain distinct, rather than making every later baptism or gift clause identical to this meal statement.

Leviticus regulates eating the flesh of a sacrifice of praise and deliverance and of vowed or freewill offerings, including the days on which it may be eaten. It supplies concrete sacrificial-meal background for Israel's altar participation; the participation formula and Paul's comparison are not additional Leviticus sentences.

The question about an idol's significance returns to the earlier explicit idol-is-nothing and one-God statement. This is an internal argument connection, preserving the question's form and the later participation warning rather than turning idol-nothingness into permission for every meal setting.

Sacrificing to demons and not God closely corresponds to Deuteronomy's same contrast. Deuteronomy additionally describes unfamiliar new gods and the fathers' lack of knowledge; Corinthians adds the warning against becoming participants with demons. The clauses and applications are not merged into one quotation.

The earlier cup-of-blessing statement identifies participation in Christ's blood and the bread's participation in His body. It supplies the named Lord-cup side of this incompatible-participation warning. The demonic cup/table contrast belongs to this later statement, not the earlier verse alone.

Deuteronomy explicitly describes God's jealousy and anger provoked by what is no god and by idols. Corinthians asks whether the readers are provoking the Lord to jealousy and whether they are stronger. The divine counter-jealousy against a nation in Deuteronomy is not inserted into Paul's shorter questions.

The same permitted/not-beneficial formulation occurs earlier, but its second limit there is not being brought under anything's authority. Here the second limit is not building up. The comparison preserves those distinct tests without assigning the repeated saying to an unnamed speaker as a documented quotation.

Both direct attention away from one's own interests toward another's. Philippians says each should look also to others' interests; Corinthians gives the own-good/other's-good contrast within food decisions. The shared other-regarding command does not make the surrounding situations identical.

The food-creation argument in Timothy calls God's creation good and rejects refusal when received with thanksgiving, sanctified through God's word and intercession. It is related to eating market meat without examination, while those stated conditions and Corinthians' later other-conscience exception remain in their own passages.

The earth belonging to the Lord and its fullness closely match the psalm's ownership declaration. The actual Psalm23:1 unit also includes its heading, the inhabited world and its dwellers. Those words are preserved in the target rather than renumbered or added to Paul's shorter food-context citation.

The earlier market-meat permission and this invitation instruction both say to eat without examining for conscience's sake. This internal comparison preserves the different market and unbeliever-household settings, and the invitation's if-you-want-to-go condition rather than requiring attendance.

Both commend abstention from food for another person's sake. Corinthians specifies an announcement that the food has been sacrificed and the informer's conscience; Romans names a brother stumbling and also includes wine. The informer is not silently identified as the same weak brother or the settings made identical.

The explicit other-conscience clarification identifies whose conscience matters in the preceding sacrifice-announcement rule. This is a direct internal explanation. The following question about freedom remains a question, rather than being rewritten as a repeal of the preceding instruction not to eat.

Both connect eating with thanksgiving. Corinthians asks why thankful participation draws slander; Romans describes both eating and abstaining for the Lord with thanks to God. The question and the paired practices remain distinct, with no identical critical incident supplied.

Both extend religious purpose to every activity. Corinthians names eating/drinking and God's glory; Colossians names word/deed, the Lord Jesus' name and thanksgiving through Him to God the Father. Their comprehensive scope corresponds while the actual purposes and named relations remain distinct.

Avoiding a cause for stumbling corresponds to Romans' command not to put a stumbling block or snare before a brother. Corinthians explicitly names Jews, Greeks and God's Church; Romans uses the brother/one-another language. Neither recipient list is substituted for the other.

The earlier all-things-to-all-people policy aims to save some; here pleasing others and seeking the many's benefit likewise aims at their salvation. This is an internal missionary-motive comparison, preserving some/many and the particular benefit language rather than asserting an independent event.
